question: What is REST and what makes an API RESTful?
title: What is REST – RESTful API Fundamentals for Java Developers
direct_answer: **REST (Representational State Transfer)** — An architectural style for designing web APIs that uses HTTP as the transport. A RESTful API identifies resources with URIs, uses HTTP methods (GET/POST/PUT/DELETE) to represent operations, and is stateless — each request contains all needed information.

interviewer_intent.testing: REST fundamentals clarity — the foundation for all backend API development
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying 'REST is a protocol' — REST is an architectural style, HTTP is the protocol
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that REST is a set of constraints (not a specification), and that an API is RESTful when it follows those constraints

sections.title: REST Architecture
sections.content:
**REST = Representational State Transfer**
- Defined by Roy Fielding in his 2000 PhD dissertation
- An architectural style — a set of design constraints
- Not a protocol (that's HTTP), not a specification (that's OpenAPI)

**Core concept: Resources**
- Everything is a resource: users, orders, products
- Resources are identified by URIs: `/users/42`, `/orders/123`
- Resources have representations: JSON, XML (JSON is the standard today)

**HTTP is the transport:**
- GET `/users/42` → retrieve user 42
- POST `/users` → create a new user
- PUT `/users/42` → update user 42
- DELETE `/users/42` → delete user 42

**What makes an API RESTful:**
- Resources identified by URIs
- Standard HTTP methods for operations
- Stateless: server doesn't store client session state
- Consistent representation format (JSON)
- Client-server separation

**What REST is NOT:**
- Not SOAP (SOAP is a protocol with its own envelope format)
- Not RPC (RPC calls functions, REST operates on resources)
- Not GraphQL (GraphQL uses a query language for flexible data fetching)

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- REST = architectural style, HTTP = protocol, OpenAPI/Swagger = specification
- Resources = nouns, HTTP methods = verbs
- Stateless: every request must carry all needed information
- URI design: `/users/{id}` not `/getUser?id=42`
- Standard responses: JSON body + appropriate HTTP status code
- Spring Boot: @RestController builds RESTful endpoints with @GetMapping, @PostMapping etc.

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: REST stands for Representational State Transfer — it's an architectural style for designing APIs, not a protocol itself. The protocol is HTTP. A RESTful API treats everything as a resource: users, orders, products — each identified by a URI. Operations on those resources are expressed using HTTP methods: GET to read, POST to create, PUT to update, DELETE to remove. The most important constraint is statelessness — the server doesn't store any client session information between requests; each request must contain everything the server needs to fulfill it. In practice, a REST API has clean URI-based resource paths, uses appropriate HTTP methods and status codes, and returns structured data — JSON in modern APIs. Spring Boot's @RestController with @GetMapping, @PostMapping, and so on is the standard way to build REST APIs in Java.

speakable_v2.hook: REST is just a set of rules for using HTTP sensibly — learn the rules and every REST API you'll ever see makes sense.

beats.text: REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style — a set of constraints — for designing web APIs over HTTP. It's not a protocol or a library. An API is 'RESTful' when it follows those constraints: statelessness, resource-based URIs, and standard HTTP methods.

Before REST, API styles like SOAP used complex XML envelopes and had their own transport rules. REST reused the HTTP protocol that browsers already understood — making APIs simpler to build, call, and cache.

items: Resource: everything is a resource — Todo, User, Order — each identified by a URI like /todos/42
HTTP method as verb: GET reads, POST creates, PUT updates, DELETE removes the resource
Stateless: each request carries all the information needed — no server-side session
JSON: standard representation format — returned in the response body

beats.text: Our todo API: GET /todos returns all todos. POST /todos with a JSON body creates one. PUT /todos/42 updates todo 42. DELETE /todos/42 removes it. In Spring Boot, @RestController on the class plus @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @DeleteMapping on methods wires this up automatically. candidates miss: REST is often confused with HTTP. HTTP is the transport protocol. REST is a design style that uses HTTP. You can build non-RESTful APIs over HTTP (like SOAP) and conversely REST could theoretically use other protocols.

items: Saying 'REST is a protocol' — it's an architectural style; HTTP is the protocol
Putting verbs in URIs like /getTodo or /createTodo — the HTTP method is the verb, URIs should be nouns

speakable_v2.cap: REST = resources (nouns) + HTTP methods (verbs) + stateless + JSON — that four-part mental model covers 90% of what you'll build.

question: What is a REST resource and how do you design URIs for it?
title: REST Resources and URI Design – Java Backend Interview
direct_answer: **REST resources** — A resource is any concept that can be named and addressed: User, Order, Product. URI design: use nouns (not verbs), plural collections, hierarchical nesting for relationships. `/users` is a collection, `/users/42` is a resource, `/users/42/orders` is a sub-resource.

interviewer_intent.testing: URI design judgment — do you know what makes a REST API consistent and predictable?
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using verbs in URIs: /getUser, /createOrder, /deleteProduct — the HTTP method is the verb
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show awareness of URI design anti-patterns and explain why the HTTP method is the verb in REST

sections.title: REST URI Design Principles
sections.content:
**Nouns, not verbs (the HTTP method IS the verb):**
```
✓ GET /users          — get all users
✓ POST /users         — create a user
✗ GET /getUsers       — verb in URI
✗ POST /createUser    — verb in URI
```

**Plural resource names:**
```
✓ /users          
✓ /orders
✗ /user
✗ /order
```

**Hierarchical relationships:**
```
/users              — all users
/users/{id}         — specific user
/users/{id}/orders  — orders belonging to this user
/users/{id}/orders/{orderId}  — specific order of this user
```

**Filtering, sorting, pagination — use query parameters:**
```
GET /users?role=ADMIN&sortBy=name&page=2&size=20
```

**Versioning:**
```
/api/v1/users
/api/v2/users  — breaking changes create new version
```

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- URIs are nouns, HTTP methods are verbs
- Use plural collection names: /users not /user
- Nested resources: /users/{id}/orders for clear ownership
- Query params for filtering, sorting, pagination — not path variables
- Lowercase with hyphens: /user-profiles not /UserProfiles
- Version your API from the start: /api/v1/

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: A resource in REST is any concept that can be addressed and operated on — users, orders, products. The URI identifies the resource, and the HTTP method expresses the operation. The key design rule is: use nouns in URIs, not verbs. The HTTP method IS the verb. So GET /orders is correct; GET /getOrders is not — you've duplicated the verb. Use plural names for collections: /users, /orders. For hierarchical relationships, nest them logically: /users/42/orders gets orders for user 42. For filtering and pagination, use query parameters, not path variables — so /users?role=admin&page=2 rather than /users/admin. And version your API from day one — /api/v1/users — because breaking changes will happen and you need a way to introduce them without breaking existing clients.

beats.text: A REST resource is any concept you can name and operate on — a Todo, a User, an Order. Each resource gets a unique URI that identifies it. The URI is a noun address; the HTTP method is the verb that says what to do with it.
Consistent URI design makes APIs predictable. When every team follows the same rules — plural nouns, nested hierarchies, query params for filtering — you can guess a URI before reading docs.

items: Collection URI: /todos — refers to all todos; POST here creates one
Instance URI: /todos/42 — refers to a specific todo; GET reads, PUT updates, DELETE removes it
Nested resource: /users/5/todos — todos belonging to user 5; expresses ownership in the path
Query params for filtering/sorting: /todos?done=false&sort=dueDate — not part of the resource path

beats.text: In our todo app: GET /todos returns the list. POST /todos with a body creates a todo. PUT /todos/42 with a body replaces it. DELETE /todos/42 removes it. GET /todos?done=false filters incomplete items. In Spring Boot, @GetMapping("/todos/{id}") with @PathVariable Long id wires the instance URI automatically. non-obvious: use lowercase hyphens for multi-word resources — /todo-items not /TodoItems or /todo_items — hyphens are the HTTP convention.

items: Verbs in URIs like /getTodo or /createTodo — the HTTP method is the verb; the URI should stay a noun
Using singular names — /todo instead of /todos — collections should be plural for consistency

speakable_v2.cap: Resource = noun with a URI. HTTP method = verb. Collection /todos, instance /todos/42, nested /users/5/todos, filters as query params — four patterns cover most URI design.

question: What is statelessness in REST and why does it matter?
title: Statelessness in REST APIs – Java Backend Interview
direct_answer: **Stateless REST** — Each request must contain ALL information needed to process it. The server stores no client context between requests. Authentication token, user ID, preferences — all in each request. Statelessness enables horizontal scaling: any server can handle any request.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of why statelessness matters for scalability — not just the definition
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying 'stateless means no database state' — databases are stateful, but server session state is what REST avoids
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect statelessness to horizontal scaling: if all state is in the request, any load balancer node can handle it without sticky sessions

sections.title: Stateless vs Stateful Request Handling
sections.content:
**Stateful (HTTP Sessions — NOT REST):**
1. Client logs in → server creates session, stores user info in memory
2. Client sends session ID in cookie
3. Server looks up session to know who the client is
4. PROBLEM: request must go to the SAME server that has the session (sticky sessions)
   OR sessions must be stored in shared store (Redis)

**Stateless (REST with JWT):**
1. Client logs in → server returns JWT containing user info
2. Client sends JWT in Authorization header with EVERY request
3. Server validates JWT, extracts user info — no DB lookup for session
4. BENEFIT: any server in the cluster can handle any request — horizontal scaling

**What stateless means practically:**
- Include authentication token in every request
- Include user preferences in the request if needed (or fetch from DB per request)
- No conversation state between requests: 'I'm on page 2 of my order flow' must be in the request

**Spring Boot:**
```java
http.sessionManagement(sm -> sm
    .sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS));  // no server sessions
```

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Stateless: server stores ZERO per-client state between requests
- Each request is independent and self-contained
- Authentication: JWT in header (not server sessions)
- Enables horizontal scaling — no sticky sessions needed
- Database is stateful — that's fine; REST doesn't say avoid databases
- Trade-off: slightly more data in each request (token overhead)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Stateless means the server doesn't remember anything about a client between requests. Every request must carry all the information the server needs to process it — including authentication. This is why REST APIs use JWT tokens: the token contains the user's identity and is sent with every request, rather than the server maintaining a session. The reason statelessness matters is scalability: if any request can be handled by any server because there's no shared session state, you can add servers behind a load balancer and all requests work the same way. Stateful APIs — those that rely on server sessions — require sticky sessions (each client must always go to the same server) or a shared session store, both of which add complexity. Statelessness removes that complexity entirely.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API for a todo app with GET, POST, PUT, DELETE endpoints
speakable_v2.hook: Stateless means the server has no memory of you between requests — every call stands on its own, which is exactly what makes scaling easy.

beats.text: Statelessness means the server stores zero per-client state between requests. Every request must carry all the information the server needs — identity, preferences, context. There is no server-side session remembering where you are in a workflow.

Stateless servers are interchangeable. If no server holds client data, a load balancer can route any request to any server. Add ten servers, remove five — clients never notice. Stateful sessions break this because the client is stuck to one server.

items: JWT in Authorization header: every request carries the token; server validates it without a DB session lookup
No server-side sessions: Spring Boot configured with SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS discards any session
Self-contained requests: if a preference matters, the client sends it or the server reads it from the DB per request
Database is still stateful: statelessness refers to the HTTP server layer only — your DB is your persistent store

beats.text: Todo app flow: user logs in, gets a JWT. Every call — GET /todos, POST /todos, DELETE /todos/42 — includes Authorization: Bearer token in the header. Any of three app servers can handle any request because none holds session state. If a server restarts, the user's next request works fine. sharp edge: stateless does not mean the app has no state — your database is stateful. The constraint is that the HTTP server layer carries no per-client memory between calls.

items: Saying stateless means no database — databases store everything; stateless is about the HTTP server layer only
Storing user context in HttpSession in a Spring REST controller — that makes the API stateful and breaks scaling

speakable_v2.cap: Stateless = no server session. Every request is self-contained with a JWT. Any server can handle any request — that's the scaling win.

question: How does Spring Boot implement a REST API?
title: Implementing REST API in Spring Boot – Java Fresher Guide
direct_answer: **Spring Boot REST** — @RestController on the class, @GetMapping/@PostMapping/@PutMapping/@DeleteMapping on methods, @PathVariable for URI params, @RequestBody for JSON input, @RequestParam for query params. ResponseEntity for explicit status codes. No XML config needed — auto-configuration handles it.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical Spring Boot REST implementation knowledge
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing @Controller (returns view names) with @RestController (returns JSON directly)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a complete endpoint with @PathVariable, @RequestBody, and ResponseEntity with appropriate status code

sections.title: Spring Boot REST Controller
Key Points
sections.content:
- @RestController = @Controller + @ResponseBody — returns JSON, not view names
- @RequestMapping at class level sets base path
- @PathVariable for /orders/{id} URI parameters
- @RequestBody for JSON request body deserialization (Jackson)
- @RequestParam for /orders?status=PENDING query parameters
- ResponseEntity<T> gives control over status codes and headers
- @Valid triggers Bean Validation on @RequestBody

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: In Spring Boot, I annotate the class with @RestController and @RequestMapping to set the base path. @RestController is shorthand for @Controller plus @ResponseBody — it tells Spring to serialize return values directly to JSON in the response, rather than treating them as view names. For each endpoint, I use the specific mapping annotation: @GetMapping for retrieval, @PostMapping for creation, @PutMapping for full updates, @DeleteMapping for deletion. Path parameters are extracted with @PathVariable, request bodies are deserialized with @RequestBody using Jackson, and query parameters with @RequestParam. For control over the HTTP status code, I return ResponseEntity — for example, 201 Created on successful POST or 204 No Content on DELETE.

How do you return a 404 when a resource is not found in Spring Boot?

question: What is the difference between a REST API and a web service?
title: REST API vs Web Service – Java Backend Interview
direct_answer: **Web service** is a broad term — any service accessible over a network. REST API is one type of web service (others: SOAP, gRPC, GraphQL). REST uses HTTP with JSON. SOAP uses XML envelope over HTTP/SMTP. gRPC uses Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2. REST has won for most web APIs; SOAP persists in enterprise/financial systems.

interviewer_intent.testing: Vocabulary precision and awareness of the broader API landscape
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using 'web service' and 'REST API' interchangeably — they're not the same
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Briefly compare REST, SOAP, and gRPC in terms of use case — shows breadth of API knowledge

sections.title: Types of Web Services
sections.content:
**Web service** = broad term: any service callable over a network

**REST API:**
- HTTP + JSON (or XML)
- Lightweight, no strict contract
- Stateless
- Dominant for web and mobile APIs
- Spring Boot, Node.js, Django all support REST

**SOAP (Simple Object Access Protocol):**
- XML envelope format
- WSDL contract (describes all operations)
- Built-in security (WS-Security), transactions, reliability
- Enterprise systems: banking, insurance, SAP integrations
- Spring WS supports SOAP if you need it

**gRPC:**
- Google's Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2
- Strongly typed schema (proto file)
- Very fast, binary format
- Excellent for microservice-to-microservice communication
- Not human-readable by default

**GraphQL:**
- Query language — client specifies exactly what data it needs
- Single endpoint (/graphql)
- Great for complex, nested, or variable data requirements

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Web service = umbrella term; REST is one type
- REST won for general web APIs — simple, lightweight, JSON
- SOAP still used in enterprise (banking, insurance, WSDL contracts)
- gRPC for high-performance microservice communication
- GraphQL for flexible client-driven data fetching
- Java supports all: Spring Boot (REST), Spring WS (SOAP), grpc-java (gRPC)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: 'Web service' is a broad term for any service accessible over a network. REST is one type of web service — the most common today for web and mobile APIs. REST uses HTTP with JSON, is stateless, and has no strict contract format. SOAP is another type — it uses XML envelopes, a formal WSDL contract, and supports advanced features like WS-Security and distributed transactions. SOAP is still used in banking and enterprise systems where those features matter. gRPC is a newer high-performance option using binary Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2 — great for microservice internal communication. GraphQL is a query language where clients specify exactly what data they need. For most new web APIs, REST is the right choice. For existing enterprise integrations, you may encounter SOAP.
